title: SEC probes Nvidia's accounting as shares plunge 14% and $500 billion vanishes in a day
summary: The US Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Nvidia's accounting practices, Reuters reported, sending the chipmaker's shares down 14 percent on Friday and wiping out roughly $500 billion of market value in a single session — its worst week in 18 years.
content:
Nvidia's terrible month has taken a turn that no investor saw coming. Shares in the world's most valuable chipmaker plunged 14 percent on Friday after Reuters reported that the US Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating the company's accounting practices, wiping out roughly $500 billion of market value in a single trading session.

The stock fell to less than $126, taking Nvidia's market capitalisation from about $3.52 trillion to about $3.03 trillion, according to The Motley Fool. The drop capped a seventh consecutive daily fall and a seventh straight weekly decline — the longest weekly losing streak since 2008, and what analysts called the company's worst week in 18 years. Shares have now lost more than 20 percent in a week.

The Wall Street Journal first reported on Tuesday that the SEC was examining Nvidia, but said it could not establish what the inquiry was about. On Friday, Reuters, citing two people briefed on the matter, reported that the agency's enforcement staff are scrutinising potential accounting issues at the company. The New York Times reported on Saturday that the inquiry is in its early stages. The SEC declined to comment, and Nvidia did not immediately respond. Reuters could not determine when the inquiry began or exactly which practices are under review.

That uncertainty is part of the problem. What is known is that two areas of Nvidia's financial reporting have already drawn public scrutiny, and either could be in the SEC's sights.

The first is how Nvidia reports where its sales come from. Last year the company changed its geographic revenue reporting, switching from customers' billing addresses to the countries where they are headquartered. On that basis, about 63 percent of last quarter's revenue came from US-based customers. The Financial Times has reported that roughly $104 billion of Nvidia's 2025 revenue was booked through its Singapore unit, and that the reporting switch came as sales billed to Singapore approached half of the company's total — an awkward look at a time when South-East Asia has become a hub for chips smuggled into China. Interim chief executive Colette Kress has said more than 99 percent of data centre revenue invoiced to Singapore came from US-based customers, but the question of where Nvidia's chips ultimately end up has only grown sharper.

The second is how Nvidia helps its customers pay for its chips. On Tuesday's earnings call, Ms Kress said Nvidia's guarantees totalled $118 billion at the end of the quarter, including $105 billion of credit support tied to a single data centre campus. Those guarantees are the kind of disclosure the SEC is watching closely across AI companies, and Nvidia's receivables are running at 64 days of sales. Scrutiny of the company's financial disclosures has also intensified around its dealings with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company investigated by American authorities over suspected shipments of restricted AI chips to China. In fiscal 2026, Nvidia recorded $19.7 billion in revenue from customers headquartered in China, mostly from permitted chips — but regulators may want to know how chips that reached China through other countries were recorded.

The probe lands on a company already in turmoil. Co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive on November 11 after revelations about his personal relationships, including one with a woman US authorities suspect of spying for China, which China denies. The board has appointed Ms Kress, the company's longtime chief financial officer, as interim chief executive and launched an investigation into the circumstances of Mr Huang's departure. He is due to testify before Congress on December 1.

Nvidia's legal troubles do not end with the SEC. The Justice Department is reviewing the company's planned $12.9 billion purchase of open-source platform Hugging Face alongside a broader antitrust investigation into its acquisitions and practices, Reuters reported last month. And the Commerce Department tightened chip export rules on November 16, requiring licences for shipments to Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil, and for data centres anywhere in the world that give Chinese companies large amounts of computing power remotely. [Nvidia has already halted shipments of its licensed H200 chips to China](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/nvidia-halts-h200-chip-shipments-china-november-2026), leaving around 600,000 processors stranded in Hong Kong.

It is worth stating plainly what an SEC investigation is and is not. It is a civil, fact-finding exercise — not a verdict, and not evidence of wrongdoing. Many such inquiries are closed without any enforcement action, and this one could end without charges being brought. The SEC under President Donald Trump has pulled back on enforcement in some areas, while saying it will focus on bread-and-butter securities fraud, including accounting violations that have long been a mainstay of its work.

Even so, the timing could hardly be worse for Nvidia's investors. The company reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion and guided the current quarter to $130 billion, but its shares have fallen every day since the earnings report, and the board's independent committee investigation is still running alongside a 10-Q filing that will follow the results in the coming weeks. The numbers, by themselves, remain extraordinary. The problem is everything around them.

The wider market has noticed. [Global technology stocks have been sliding as the AI rally falters](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/global-stocks-worst-run-since-2023-ai-selloff-november-2026), and Nvidia — the company that came to symbolise the AI boom — is now its most visible casualty. The investigations now surrounding the company are likely to hang over it for months, and the questions investors are asking have shifted from how fast Nvidia can grow to whether its books, its governance and its China business can withstand the scrutiny now arriving from Washington. [Reuters has the full account of the SEC inquiry and what is known about its focus](https://live.euronext.com/en/financial-news/nvidias-accounting-focus-us-sec-investigation-sources-say).
